questions.q: What does the TCP/IP model's Application layer roughly correspond to in the OSI model?
options: Only OSI's Application layer (Layer 7)
OSI's Application, Presentation, and Session layers (7, 6, and 5)
OSI's Physical layer (Layer 1)
All seven OSI layers combined
questions.explain: TCP/IP collapses OSI's top three layers — Application, Presentation, and Session — into a single Application layer, since in practice one protocol usually handles all three jobs.

questions.q: Which transport protocol guarantees ordered, reliable delivery and is the right choice for a file download?
options: UDP
TCP
DNS
DHCP
questions.explain: TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees delivery and order, retransmitting lost data — exactly what a file download needs to arrive intact.

questions.q: What happens in TCP's three-way handshake, in order?
options: ACK, then SYN, then SYN-ACK
SYN, then SYN-ACK, then ACK
SYN-ACK, then ACK, then SYN
There is no fixed order — TCP sends data immediately
questions.explain: The client sends SYN, the server responds SYN-ACK, and the client finishes with ACK — only then is the connection established and data allowed to flow.

questions.q: Why is UDP typically the better choice for a live video call rather than TCP?
options: UDP guarantees every frame arrives in order
UDP is connection-oriented, which suits real-time media
A dropped frame that arrives late is worse than one simply skipped, and UDP's lack of retransmission avoids that delay
TCP cannot carry video data at all
questions.explain: UDP sends data without waiting for acknowledgment or retransmitting lost packets, which keeps a live stream moving smoothly instead of stalling to recover a frame that's already too late to matter.

questions.q: Why do networking professionals still use both the OSI and TCP/IP models in everyday conversation?
options: Because the two models are identical, so it doesn't matter which term is used
OSI's seven-layer granularity is useful for precise troubleshooting language, while TCP/IP's four layers more closely match how real software stacks are organized
TCP/IP has been officially retired and OSI is the only model still in use
Because job interviews require memorizing both, but neither is used on the job
questions.explain: OSI gives more precise troubleshooting vocabulary (distinguishing Layer 1 from Layer 2, for example), while TCP/IP more closely mirrors how an actual device's network stack is built — so both stay in active use.
